lessons.title: Factors that affect Azure costs
lessons.summary: Understand choices that influence Azure spending, including resource type, size, runtime, storage, and usage patterns.
learningObjectives: Identify cost drivers such as resource size, runtime, storage, data transfer, and support
Explain how consumption-based usage affects Azure spending
Recognize how budgets, tags, and right-sizing help control cost
lessons.explanation:
Azure cost management begins with understanding that many services follow a consumption model. Costs are affected by what you deploy, how large it is, how long it runs, how much data is stored or moved, and which support, licensing, or Marketplace choices apply. A virtual machine that runs all month usually costs more than one stopped when not needed. Larger resource sizes usually cost more than smaller suitable sizes. Storage redundancy, transactions, and network traffic can also affect spend.

Cost is not only a finance topic. Architects and operators influence cost by right-sizing resources, removing unused items, choosing appropriate redundancy, and reviewing recommendations. Microsoft Cost Management helps analyze actual spending, while Azure Advisor can surface optimization opportunities. Tags support reporting by business meaning, but tags only help when teams use them consistently and act on the reports.

terminology.definition: Using and paying for cloud resources based on measured usage.
A service tier or size that defines capabilities and can influence cost.
A Cost Management setting that tracks spend against a threshold.

lessons.recap: Understand choices that influence Azure spending, including resource type, size, runtime, storage, and usage patterns. Focus on purpose, scope, and when to use each tool.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of Azure cost like planning a delivery route. The size of the truck, distance traveled, toll roads, waiting time, and unused space all affect the bill; choosing carefully matters more than memorizing a single price.

lessons.title: Pricing calculator, Cost Management, and tags
lessons.summary: Estimate planned costs, monitor actual costs, and group resources with tags.
learningObjectives: Choose Pricing Calculator for estimates and Cost Management for actual spend
Explain how tags group resources for cost analysis and ownership
Identify when budgets and alerts help monitor Azure spending
lessons.explanation:
Cost work happens in stages. Before deployment, the Azure pricing calculator helps create an estimate from anticipated services and usage. It is useful for planning, but it is not a guarantee of the invoice because actual cost follows measured usage, discounts, and later configuration changes. After resources exist, Microsoft Cost Management helps analyze, monitor, alert on, export, and optimize actual spend.

Tags add business metadata such as Environment, Owner, Application, or CostCenter. Tags can make cost reports more meaningful, but they must be applied consistently. Tags are stored as plain text and should not contain secrets or sensitive values. A beginner-friendly pattern is: estimate first, deploy with tags, set budgets and alerts, then review Cost Management and Advisor recommendations.

misconception.myth: The calculator guarantees the final invoice.
misconception.reality: It estimates from inputs; actual usage and billing details determine cost.

lessons.examTakeaway: Calculator means planning; Cost Management means actual spend; tags mean organization and allocation.
lessons.recap: Estimate planned costs, monitor actual costs, and group resources with tags. Focus on purpose, scope, and when to use each tool.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of the pricing calculator as a shopping estimate, Cost Management as the receipt and spending dashboard, and tags as colored labels that show which team or project put items in the basket.

lessons.title: Azure Policy and resource locks
lessons.summary: Use Azure Policy for governance standards and resource locks for protection against accidental deletion or changes.
learningObjectives: Distinguish Azure Policy governance effects from resource lock protection
Identify when policies enforce allowed regions, tags, or compliance standards
Choose CanNotDelete or ReadOnly locks to prevent accidental changes
lessons.explanation:
Azure Policy evaluates resources against business rules. A policy definition describes a condition and an effect such as audit, deny, modify, or deploy related settings. Assignments apply definitions or initiatives at scopes such as management groups, subscriptions, or resource groups. Policy is useful for allowed regions, required tags, diagnostic settings, and compliance dashboards.

Resource locks solve a different problem. A lock can apply to a subscription, resource group, or resource to prevent deletion or modification. Portal lock names are Delete and Read-only; command-line names are CanNotDelete and ReadOnly. Locks override normal permissions for management operations, so they should be documented and used carefully.

Use Policy to evaluate and enforce standards across many resources. Use locks to protect important scopes from accidental administrative action.

terminology.definition: A rule that Azure Policy evaluates.
A collection of policy definitions assigned together.
A lock that blocks deletion.
A lock that blocks deletion and many management updates.

misconception.myth: Azure Policy and locks are interchangeable.
misconception.reality: Policy governs compliance rules; locks protect management operations on scopes.

lessons.examTakeaway: Standards or compliance dashboard means Policy; accidental deletion or update protection means lock.
lessons.recap: Use Azure Policy for governance standards and resource locks for protection against accidental deletion or changes. Focus on purpose, scope, and when to use each tool.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of Azure Policy as a building code inspector and a resource lock as a padlock on a door. The inspector checks whether new work follows standards; the padlock helps prevent accidental changes or deletion.
lessons.anotherExample: A platform team can assign a policy requiring approved regions, then place a delete lock on a critical production resource group during a migration weekend.

lessons.title: Microsoft Purview and the Service Trust Portal
lessons.summary: Distinguish data governance in Microsoft Purview from trust and compliance evidence in the Service Trust Portal.
learningObjectives: Distinguish Microsoft Purview data governance from Service Trust Portal compliance evidence
Identify Purview catalog and lineage capabilities for data assets
Choose Service Trust Portal for audit reports and compliance documents
lessons.explanation:
Microsoft Purview helps organizations govern data by improving visibility, discovery, quality, lineage, and business context. Data Map and Unified Catalog focus on metadata: what data exists, where it came from, who owns it, and how it should be used. These capabilities help governance but do not automatically grant access to the underlying data.

The Microsoft Service Trust Portal serves a different purpose. It provides audit reports, compliance information, whitepapers, and artifacts about Microsoft cloud services. Some resources require sign-in with a Microsoft Entra organization account and acceptance of terms.

For fundamentals, keep the tool selection clear. Choose Purview when the scenario asks about cataloging, lineage, or governing data assets. Choose the Service Trust Portal when it asks for Microsoft compliance documentation, audit reports, or trust resources.

lessons.title: Azure portal, Cloud Shell, CLI, PowerShell, and Azure Arc
lessons.summary: Choose the right Azure management tool for graphical tasks, browser commands, scripting, and hybrid management.
learningObjectives: Choose portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI, or Azure PowerShell for management tasks
Distinguish browser-based management from repeatable scripting tools
Identify when Azure Arc extends management to hybrid resources
lessons.explanation:
Azure provides multiple management experiences because teams work in different ways. The Azure portal is a browser-based graphical console for creating, configuring, monitoring, and managing resources. Azure Cloud Shell is an authenticated browser terminal that offers Bash or PowerShell with Azure tools available. Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool using `az` commands, while Azure PowerShell is the Az module for administrators who prefer PowerShell cmdlets and objects.

Azure Arc extends management and governance to supported resources outside Azure, such as servers or Kubernetes clusters, by projecting them into Azure Resource Manager. For AZ-900, choose the tool by workflow: visual portal, browser shell, command-line script, PowerShell automation, or hybrid governance.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code: ARM templates and Bicep
lessons.summary: Use ARM templates and Bicep to make Azure deployments repeatable, reviewable, and consistent.
learningObjectives: Explain how ARM templates and Bicep make Azure deployments repeatable
Distinguish declarative infrastructure files from manual portal changes
Recognize why source control and reviews improve deployment consistency
lessons.explanation:
Infrastructure as code means defining cloud infrastructure in files instead of relying only on manual portal clicks. The file can be stored, reviewed, versioned, and reused with the project. Azure Resource Manager templates are JSON files that declare resources and configuration. You state what should exist, and Resource Manager orchestrates the deployment.

Bicep is a domain-specific language for Azure resources. It offers a more concise authoring experience than JSON while using the same underlying Resource Manager deployment capabilities. Both ARM templates and Bicep are declarative and support repeatable results. IaC helps teams reduce drift between environments, review infrastructure changes, and rebuild environments more reliably.

lessons.title: Azure Advisor and Azure Service Health
lessons.summary: Differentiate optimization recommendations from personalized platform health communications.
learningObjectives: Distinguish Azure Advisor recommendations from Azure Service Health notifications
Identify Advisor categories for cost, security, reliability, performance, and operations
Choose Service Health alerts for platform incidents or planned maintenance
lessons.explanation:
Azure Advisor is a recommendation service. It analyzes resource configuration and usage telemetry, then suggests ways to improve reliability, security, performance, cost, and operational excellence. Use Advisor when you ask how to improve resources you already run.

Azure Service Health answers a different question: is Azure experiencing an issue or upcoming maintenance that may affect me? It brings together Azure Status, Service Health, and Resource Health. Azure Status is a broad public view. Service Health provides personalized communications about incidents, planned maintenance, and advisories for services and regions you use. Resource Health focuses on individual resource availability.

Use Advisor for optimization guidance. Use Service Health to stay informed about platform events and configure relevant alerts.

lessons.recap: Differentiate optimization recommendations from personalized platform health communications. Focus on purpose, scope, and when to use each tool.

lessons.title: Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, and alerts
lessons.summary: Understand Azure Monitor telemetry, Log Analytics queries, and alerts with action groups.
learningObjectives: Describe how Azure Monitor collects metrics, logs, traces, and events
Distinguish metrics from logs and Log Analytics queries
Identify when alerts and action groups notify teams about resource conditions
lessons.explanation:
Azure Monitor is Microsoft's unified observability service for collecting, analyzing, and acting on telemetry from cloud and hybrid environments. It brings together metrics, logs, traces, and events so teams can understand health, performance, and reliability. Metrics are numerical measurements over time, useful for trends and thresholds. Logs contain detailed records that can be queried.

Log Analytics is the Azure portal tool used to run and edit queries against Azure Monitor Logs, including Kusto Query Language mode for advanced analysis. Alerts help teams respond before users report a problem. An alert rule watches a resource signal, evaluates a condition, and fires when the condition is met. Action groups then notify people or trigger automation. AZ-900 expects you to recognize these building blocks, not write complex queries.

lessons.businessScenario: Litware needs to know when performance degrades and investigate detailed log records.
lessons.technicalExample: The team creates metric alerts and uses Log Analytics queries for investigation.

misconception.myth: Monitoring is only useful after an outage ends.
misconception.reality: Monitoring helps detect, investigate, and respond while issues are developing.

lessons.examTakeaway: Metrics, logs, Log Analytics, alerts, and action groups are the Azure Monitor basics.
lessons.recap: Understand Azure Monitor telemetry, Log Analytics queries, and alerts with action groups. Focus on purpose, scope, and when to use each tool.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of Azure Monitor like a building control room. Metrics are quick gauge readings, logs are detailed event records, and alerts are rules that call someone when a reading or pattern needs attention.
lessons.anotherExample: An operations team can alert when CPU remains high, then query logs in Log Analytics to see which requests or errors happened at the same time.
